report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Synopsis

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026 a 220 t class rigid haul truck, HT-407, descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine empty, struck the right side of a light vehicle, LV-118, as it came out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. All times in this report are local time (UTC+8). The haul truck operator braked from 37 km/h and the truck struck at 24 km/h. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow. Its one occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor on a third night shift, sustained "a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax". The technician was conscious throughout, was extricated through the rear at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The light vehicle was destroyed and the truck returned to service on 14/08/2026. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury (ORR-OCC-2026-0332). [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the haul truck operator was injured]. Drug and alcohol tests on the haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor were negative.

The spur was cut under a works order classified as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised and nothing went to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department or the technical services group, which very likely contributed to two later conditions. The intersection had a 41 m sight line against a 96 m stopping distance and no stop control or warning sign, which likely contributed to the light vehicle driving out without stopping. A collision awareness geofence suppressed alerts at the spur and operators did not know of it. This likely contributed through the haul truck operator's expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp, although the alert would have added little warning. The plan required a positive call only at nine listed intersections and the spur was not one, so it was very likely that this contributed to neither driver calling. The light vehicle driver's card had been issued with no check of the pit driving assessment, which likely contributed. The guideline's lack of a review trigger and of a basis for nominating call intersections likely contributed too, at the standard of proof and no higher. Together these left neither driver aware of the other until about six seconds remained.

The haul truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon appearing, which cut the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h. Whether airborne dust affected the sighting could not be determined, and the extrication delay was unlikely to have affected the outcome.

The Mining Manager issued a direction at 05:10 on 12/08/2026 requiring a positive call at every Stage 4 intersection until further notice. The investigator in charge made three recommendations on works orders, the route onto the call list between reviews, and geofence changes.

Factual information

History of the occurrence

The RL 312 spur was a 240 m access road to dewatering bore DW-14 at RL 312 in the Stage 4 pit at Bindarra Gold Mine. It was cut under works order WO-26-4471, raised on 28/07/2026, which recorded the earthworks complete on 31/07/2026. The spur was opened to light vehicles on 02/08/2026, when DW-14 was energised. A sign reading "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" had stood at the spur mouth while the road was cut. The works log recorded it removed the same day, and nothing was installed in its place. No sign, give-way control or delineation was added afterwards.

At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026 a dewatering technician came out of the spur in front of a descending haul truck about 60 m away, reversed back into the spur and let the truck pass. The technician submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 the same night. The Dewatering Superintendent closed it on 06/08/2026 with an entry that the crew had been reminded to take care, and the risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low on closure. The report was not referred to the mining department, the contractor, the survey department or the traffic management plan owner.

On 09/08/2026 the gatehouse issued a site access card to the light vehicle driver, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor. The card followed a 20 minute briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. The first of the driver's three night shifts at Bindarra began that evening, and the other two were on 10/08 and 11/08.

On 12/08/2026 dispatch called Stage 4 back to work from crib at 02:22:41. HT-407, a 220 t class rigid haul truck, began its first cycle after crib and loaded for the ROM pad. The pit channel was logged continuously, and the investigator listened to the whole period from the return from crib to two minutes after the collision. HT-407 called, and was acknowledged, at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28, at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37 and at the RL 360 crossover going down at 02:46:21. The recording contains no transmission by either vehicle about the RL 312 spur, the dewatering bore or a light vehicle being in the Stage 4 pit.

The light vehicle, LV-118, was at the DW-14 collar at RL 312, where the driver finished a set of levels. Its movements before the spur mouth were estimated from the driver's account and the length of the spur. On that basis the driver drove the 240 m spur from about 02:45 to about 02:47 and reached the mouth at 02:47. Nobody on the shift knew that a light vehicle was in the pit, because there was no permit, call-in or board by which they could.

HT-407 was returning empty down the main ramp for its second load. The truck's download shows its last steady data point at 02:47:06.0, at 37 km/h and 53 m above the spur mouth. At 02:47:07.4, 38.5 m above the mouth, service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, the retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied. At 02:47:09.2 the collision awareness system logged a proximity event with the light vehicle at 21.4 m and suppressed the alert, so nothing was presented in the cab.

The impact was at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth. LV-118 was turning right out of the spur to go up the ramp, across the descending lane, with its right side towards the truck. The front left of the truck struck the right side of the light vehicle, pushed it 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled it onto its left side against the inner windrow. The truck stopped 19 m below the intersection at about 02:47:19.

Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic at 02:48:01, 49 seconds after the collision and 20 seconds after the haul truck operator's first call. Dispatch told the operator to stay in the cab until the ramp was stopped, and released the operator at 02:48:44. The operator then went down to the light vehicle and stayed with the driver until the emergency response team arrived. The night shift supervisor, who was at the ROM pad when the call came, said over the radio that the supervisor was five minutes away.

On the radio the operator reported that the driver was conscious and talking, and could not get out because the door was against the ground. The supervisor told the operator not to move the driver and to wait for the emergency response team.

Injuries to persons

One person was seriously injured, the light vehicle driver, who was the only occupant of LV-118. The driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The driver was conscious throughout, was treated at the surface medical facility and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the number of occupants of HT-407 and any injury to them]

Damage

LV-118 was destroyed. Its roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached. The driver's seatbelt was found fastened, and its webbing carried loading marks. Damage to the light vehicle was concentrated on the right side from the B pillar forward.

Damage to HT-407 was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder, with nothing above the bumper line. The truck returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours.

Personnel information

Haul truck operator

The haul truck operator had 14 months at Bindarra, 4 years 2 months with Tarrowen Mining Services, 7 years on 220 t class rigid haul trucks and 11 years in open pit mining. The operator held a verification of competency on the 220 t class unit issued in 06/2025 and current, completed an annual refresher in 02/2026, and completed the site general induction in 06/2025. The training file shows no traffic management refresher since that induction. The induction module on traffic management is a 23 slide package that names the nine Appendix B intersections and does not say what to do at an intersection that is not listed. No training on the collision awareness system's suppression geofences was recorded anywhere on site for any person.

The operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing, and the collision was 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift. The operator's own sleep log, kept voluntarily and provided by the operator, gives 6 hours 30 minutes of sleep in the day before the occurrence and between 5 and 7 hours on each of the preceding nine days. The roster was 14 nights on and 7 off, from 18:00 to 06:30 with a 30 minute crib. The contractor's fatigue management standard sets a maximum of 14 consecutive night shifts and a minimum 10 hour break, and both were met. Site access records show the previous nine shifts worked in sequence, with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes. A drug and alcohol test taken after the occurrence was negative.

Light vehicle driver

The collision was on the driver's third night shift at Bindarra. The driver had completed the Hallorn online general induction, a two hour module, on 24/07/2026. The access card was issued on 09/08/2026 against Hallorn's recognition agreement. The training file and the gatehouse register show no entry for the Bindarra site-specific supplement and none for the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, and the gatehouse did not ask for either. The driver's account was that the driver had never seen BIN-TMP-004.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site-specific supplement was issued, because Hallorn's own records are outstanding]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the light vehicle driver's drug and alcohol result, age, licence and previous mining experience]

Night shift supervisor

The night shift supervisor had 2 years 6 months in the role, 8 years with Tarrowen Mining Services and 19 years in open pit mining. On night shift the supervisor was responsible for the haul fleet, the excavators, the ancillary fleet, the dozers and the dispatch operator. The supervisor was not responsible for the dewatering crew, the survey contractor, the drill and blast crew when on days, or any other light vehicle in the pit. The supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the Stage 4 pit that night. A drug and alcohol test taken after the occurrence was negative.

Equipment information

HT-407 was a 220 t class rigid haul truck, commissioned in 03/2021, with 31,480 engine hours and a last 500 hour service on 28/07/2026 with no defects carried. The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026 gave a mean deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 net, empty on a 9 per cent descending grade. A test on 14/08/2026, before the unit returned to service, gave 0.82 m/s2 net on the same grade. The retarder, service brakes and park brake met specification before and after the occurrence. The pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 was complete and recorded no defects. No defect was raised against the lighting, mirrors, cameras or cab glass in the twelve months before the occurrence.

LV-118 was a 4WD utility, in service from 02/2024, with 61,200 km and a last periodic service on 17/07/2026. It was fitted with a certified roll-over protection structure, a 4.5 m amber beacon whip, reflective marking to the site standard and a UHF radio. The inspection sheet for the week of 09/08/2026 recorded all items serviceable. LV-118 was not dispatched and carried no fleet management system, and its collision awareness transponder was a passive tag. The beacon lamp was tested after recovery and worked, and the whip was sheared at its base.

Site and intersection information

At RL 312 the main ramp ran on a 9.1 per cent descending grade, 24 m wide between windrows, and its surface was dry and well maintained. Traffic kept left, so a descending truck ran on the open, pit side of the road. The spur joined the ramp on a descending truck's left, on the inside of a left-hand bend, at an included angle of 71 degrees. It was cut to a formed width of 8 m with windrows to both sides. The spur mouth was 34 m below a convex grade break where the descent steepens, which the crews called the crest.

The mine survey department picked up the intersection on 13/08/2026 (SUR-26-1188). It reported:

  • "An operator descending the ramp, seated at an eye height of 5.80 m above the running surface, first has line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m."
  • "The top of a 4.5 m beacon whip on a light vehicle approaching the mouth in the spur is in view from the same eye height from 53 m, over the grade break and above the windrow; the vehicle's body is not."
  • "A driver at the spur mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first has line of sight to a descending truck at 38 m; the inner windrow, 1.6 m high, stands between the spur and the ramp for the last 25 m of the spur's approach and takes the truck's lower body out of view before that."

The survey gave the stopping distance of a 220 t class truck travelling empty at the posted 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descending grade, calculated with the manufacturer's data and a 1.5 second response, as 96 m. It gave the plan's minimum sight distance as 120 m and the available sight distance at the intersection as 41 m.

At the time of the occurrence the intersection had no intersection warning sign on either ramp approach, no give-way or stop control at the spur mouth, no delineation, reflective marker posts or windrow gap markers, and no posted speed for the spur.

The in-cab road network for the Stage 4 pit was last published on 24/07/2026 and did not contain the spur. The display therefore showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312 on the night. Publishing a revised road network is a survey task raised by a management of change record, and none existed for the spur.

Meteorology and conditions

The occurrence was in darkness. There was no fixed lighting anywhere in the Stage 4 pit. The only lighting was vehicle lighting and the light plants at the loading face, 1.1 km away and out of sight behind the crest. Moonset was at 23:18 the previous evening. The Bindarra met station recorded wind south-east at 8 km/h, a temperature of 9 degrees and no precipitation. The last rainfall at the site was 26 days before the occurrence. The investigator examined the ramp at 06:20 and found it dry throughout, with no damp patches, ponding or greasy film at or above the intersection.

The water cart log shows the main ramp between RL 280 and RL 400 was last watered at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the occurrence. The standing night shift instruction was a ramp pass every 90 minutes, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench beside the ramp, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval. The shift mean was 88 and the site trigger was 250. The reading was described as "a measure of airborne particulate at the monitor head", and it was noted that "Nothing at Bindarra measures visibility" and that "no measurement exists of what could be seen from either cab on the night."

Recorded information

Truck download

The fleet management system download for HT-407 shows the truck descending the main ramp empty at 39 km/h at RL 384 and 38 km/h at RL 351, with the retarder on its second position. It was at 37 km/h at its last steady data point at RL 317. The interval from that data point to the first rise in brake pressure was 1.4 seconds. Speed was 32 km/h at RL 314, 21.4 m above the spur mouth, and 24 km/h at the intersection. The accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal at the impact.

Mean deceleration from the brake application to the collision was 0.78 m/s2 net of the grade, from 37 km/h to 24 km/h over 4.6 seconds and 39 m of road. The retarder and the service brakes performed as specified throughout. The impact and the push took the truck to about 20 km/h, and it came to rest about seven seconds after the collision with the park brake applied.

Collision awareness system

The collision awareness system log reports the system on HT-407 as follows:

  • "System operating at Level 8 (operator advisory). Level 9 (automated intervention) is available on this fleet and is not enabled at Bindarra."
  • "Advisory alerts are raised on a vehicle tag entering the 60 m detection ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, except inside a suppression geofence."
  • "Inside a suppression geofence no alert is raised at any range, and the system logs a proximity event only once the range falls below 25 m."

The suppression geofence S4-LOAD was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the Stage 4 loading face to stop nuisance alerts between the excavator, the trucks and the service vehicles working in the same area. It was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the loading face advanced, which carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time. The extended boundary lies 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 spur intersection, so the intersection sits inside the suppressed area. The contractor's technical services group made the extension as a system configuration task. It is not recorded in the traffic management plan and was not reviewed against it.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the size of the S4-LOAD extension of 09/06/2026, because the configuration gives the new boundary and not the old one]

The event log holds three entries for the occurrence. The first is the proximity event at 02:47:09.2, 2.8 seconds before the collision, logged as "range 21.4 m closing 32 km/h", in zone S4-LOAD, with "alert SUPPRESSED (geofence)". It was logged then because that was when the range fell below 25 m. The second is the impact, logged by the accelerometer at 1.9 g longitudinal. The third is a further proximity event at "range 0.0 m", also suppressed, 0.1 seconds after the impact.

Alert statistics

In the 12 months to 11/08/2026 HT-407 raised 1,684 operator advisory alerts, all outside the S4-LOAD geofence and none inside it. Across the Stage 4 haul fleet, 68 proximity events were logged inside the geofence and suppressed. Nine of the 68 involved a light vehicle tag on the main ramp below the geofence boundary, and all nine are dated after 09/06/2026. The technical services group's standing report covers alert counts and system health and does not report suppressed events, and nobody had queried them.

Pit channel recording

Beyond the calls already described, LV-118 made no transmission on the pit channel that shift other than logging on at 18:04, at the start of shift. After the collision the haul truck operator called the collision to dispatch twice, the second time asking for the emergency response team. Dispatch told the operator, "Negative 407, stay in the cab until I've stopped the traffic."

Scene marks

The scene was examined before recovery (INV-2026-0332-SCENE). The braked tyre scuff of HT-407's left front tyre started 38.5 m up-ramp of the spur mouth and ran 58 m to the truck's resting position. It deviated 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m, consistent with the 14 degree steering input on the download. The impact position was 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow.

A continuous gouge ran 18.4 m down-ramp from the impact position. It changed at 11.2 m from tyre scuff to body panel gouge, which is where the vehicle went over. LV-118 came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, 18.4 m down-ramp of the impact position and facing down-ramp. Right-side glass and mirror fragments lay from 4.8 m to 14 m down-ramp of the impact position, and the sheared beacon whip was recovered 9 m from the vehicle.

Organisational and management information

External requirements

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 revision 4 was issued by the State Mines Inspectorate in 2021 under regulation 6.22 of the Mining Operations Safety Regulations 2018. Compliance with it is one way of discharging the regulation, which itself requires that "the operator shall manage the risks arising from the interaction of vehicles at the mine". The guideline provides, at clause 3.2:

  • "The operator shall prepare and maintain a traffic management plan for the mine. The plan shall be reviewed at intervals not exceeding twelve months, and following any significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern." (MSG-14 clause 3.2)

At clause 5.1 it provides:

  • "The operator shall nominate the intersections, crossings and other interaction zones at the mine at which positive communication between vehicles is required before entry, and shall record them in the plan." (MSG-14 clause 5.1)

Clause 3.5 makes the plan a site document, not approved by the Inspectorate and not required to be submitted except on request after an occurrence or an inspection. Clause 5.4 requires that where a light vehicle and a heavy vehicle may interact, the light vehicle be detectable by the heavy vehicle operator, by line of sight, elevated marking, radio communication, a proximity detection system or a combination of these. The guideline does not define "significant change" and gives no example of one. It does not say who nominates the interaction zones or on what basis, and it sets no minimum. It does not say which of the five means at clause 5.4 must be provided, or how many.

Traffic management plan

Bindarra Traffic Management Plan BIN-TMP-004 revision 7 was owned by the Mining Manager, Orrabinda Resources, issued on 12/11/2025 and due for review on 12/11/2026. It provides:

  • "Light vehicles shall give way to heavy vehicles at all times and in all circumstances." (clause 4.1)
  • "A positive call shall be made on the relevant pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B, and entry shall not be made until the call is acknowledged or the channel is confirmed clear." (clause 4.3.1)
  • "At intersections not listed at Appendix B, vehicles shall give way in accordance with clause 4.1. No call is required." (clause 4.3.2)
  • "At every intersection, the available sight distance shall be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle using the road at the posted speed, and in no case less than 120 m. Where this cannot be achieved, the intersection shall be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller." (clause 6.2)
  • "Every intersection shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 shall be provided with an intersection warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road, and delineation at the mouth." (clause 6.4)
  • "This plan shall be reviewed annually, and following any significant change to the mine's road network." (clause 9.1)

Appendix B lists nine intersections requiring positive communication: the ROM pad turn-off, the RL 360 crossover, the Stage 2 ramp junction, the Stage 2 dump access, the Stage 3 ramp junction, the workshop apron entry, the explosives magazine access, the raw water pump station access and the light vehicle parking bay at RL 400. The note to Appendix B provides that the appendix is reviewed and reissued at the annual review, and that an intersection is added where it appears on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 and the review assesses it as requiring positive communication. Schedule 1 is dated 12/11/2025 and is reissued at the annual review.

The RL 312 spur appears on neither document, so clause 6.4 did not apply to it. No provision in the plan allows an intersection to be added to Appendix B or Schedule 1 between annual reviews, and none requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner when it is cut. Appendix B is reproduced on a laminated board in each crib room, and the board in the Stage 4 crib room was the 12/11/2025 issue.

Annual reviews were completed on 14/11/2023, 10/11/2024 and 12/11/2025, and each reissued Schedule 1 and Appendix B. No out-of-cycle review had been carried out under clause 9.1 in the plan's eleven year history. The survey department's road register shows 14 new roads cut in the Stage 4 pit since the 12/11/2025 review, 11 under a works order and 3 under a management of change record. All three raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner, and none of the 11 raised under a works order was.

Management of change and works orders

Management of change procedure ORR-PRO-022 revision 3 provides:

  • "A management of change record shall be raised before any of the following: a change to the mine's road network; the introduction of a new vehicle type; a change to a pit design; a change to a documented control." (clause 5.2)
  • "Clause 5.2 does not apply to routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced. Such work is managed under the works order." (clause 5.3)
  • "Where a management of change record is raised, the change owner shall complete the impact assessment at Schedule 2, which includes referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration." (clause 5.4)

The works order form at Schedule 4 has no equivalent fields and no referral of any kind.

Works order WO-26-4471 was raised by the Mining Engineer on 28/07/2026 and approved by the Mining Superintendent on 29/07/2026. It classified the work as follows:

  • "Routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design. No new plant or vehicle type. Management of change not required, ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3."

Its handover field read "N/A". The works order carried no scope for signage, no survey pickup of the new intersection, no referral to the traffic management plan, no request to publish a revised road network and no review of the collision awareness system geofences. None of the three referrals listed at clause 5.4 was made.

Contractor management

Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 revision 5, clause 7.3, allows a contractor's own general induction to be accepted as equivalent to the Bindarra general induction where the contractor holds a current recognition agreement. Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical had held one since 2023. The standard provides:

  • "Equivalence under 7.3 does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement, or to the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted." (clause 7.4)
  • "The engaging department is responsible for verifying that 7.4 has been completed before a site access card is issued." (clause 7.5)

The gatehouse issued cards against the recognition agreement alone, held no record of the supplement or the pit driving assessment, and was not asked for one. Nothing in the access card system distinguished a person who might drive in an operating pit from one who might not.

Earlier hazard reports

A search of Orrabinda Resources reports raised at Bindarra in the 24 months to 11/08/2026 returned four reports, including HAZ-2026-0917. The other three, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, each described a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at an intersection not listed at Appendix B, at three different locations. The department that received each report closed all four within three days, with an entry that the crew had been reminded to take care and that heavy vehicles have right of way. None was referred to the traffic management plan owner, and none resulted in a change to Appendix B, to Schedule 1 or to any physical control.

Emergency response

The following is taken from the emergency response log and the post-incident review. The night shift was rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic, who was at the surface medical facility. A second responder, who must be present before any extrication is begun, was called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse. The second responder travelled in the second response vehicle, which was garaged at the village and carried the hydraulic rescue tool.

Dispatch paged the emergency response team at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54, and the second responder arrived with the tool at 03:07. The driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and reached the surface medical facility at 03:41.

The post-incident review found the extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes, waiting for the second responder and the tool. It measured the delay from 02:58, when the paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made, to the second responder's arrival at 03:07. The review recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome on this occasion because the injuries were stable and the patient was conscious throughout.

Other information

The notification of the occurrence listed the following immediate actions:

  • The Stage 4 pit was stood down, the main ramp was closed below RL 340 and the RL 312 spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic.
  • Both vehicles were isolated and left in position, and the scene was photographed and surveyed before recovery.
  • The haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor were stood down for the remainder of the shift.
  • The contractor's technical services group downloaded the fleet management system and collision awareness system data from HT-407 at 09:30 and provided it to the investigation unopened.
  • The Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 requiring a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, listed in the plan or not, until further notice.

Accounts of those involved

Haul truck operator

The haul truck operator was interviewed. The operator described coming down empty at thirty-seven or thirty-eight, with the retarder on and little use of the brakes, and said a glow appeared on the road above the crest and then the beacon whip came up over it. The operator braked and steered in the same movement, towards the wall on the right, because the left was the open edge and "a hundred and something metres down". The operator said the first sight was "I'd say forty metres." The survey places the beacon first in view at 53 m and the notification gives about 53 m. The operator's estimate of about forty metres is lower than that figure.

Asked about the spur, the operator said, "I thought it was still closed. There was a closed sign on it." The operator had noticed the sign was gone without thinking anything of it. Of the in-cab screen the operator said, "There's no road there on the screen. There's no intersection marked, nothing."

On the collision awareness system the operator said, "I've never had it go off down there. Not once." The operator had been on the pit for fourteen months and said that on the haul road it sounded two or three times a shift. The operator took the quiet below the crest to mean there was nothing to alert on. In the interview the operator said the supervisor told the operator afterwards that the system was switched off there.

On radio calls the operator said the list was in the crib room and that at an intersection not on it, "You don't call." The operator made no call before the spur because, as far as the operator knew, it was a closed road off the side of the ramp.

On dust the operator said, "There's always a bit of dust. The cart had been through earlier but it dries out. There was some hanging around, yeah." The operator added that the operator could not say whether it made a difference. On fatigue the operator said, "Tired, the way you are on night ten. Not falling asleep tired." The operator reported six and a half hours of sleep that day and said, "I was awake and I was driving properly."

The operator also submitted a safety report under a confidential reporting scheme. It gave the same estimate of about forty metres at first sight and the same account of braking and steering right into the windrow. It also set out three points the operator wished to put on record. The operator knew the road had been cut but did not know it was open, because the closed sign had gone and nothing was said, and it was not on the in-cab screen. The operator made no call before the spur because it was not on the crib room list, and the operator said every operator on the pit would describe the same rule. The collision awareness system had never sounded in the pit in fourteen months, the operator had taken that to mean the pit was empty, and the operator learned the day after the collision that it was switched off there.

Night shift supervisor

The night shift supervisor was interviewed, and the account below is from the investigator's write-up. The supervisor said that nobody told the supervisor when a light vehicle was in the pit, and that no book, call or permit existed for it. The supervisor knew the spur had been cut and that the dewatering crew used it, but never thought of it as an intersection and described it as one of forty similar tracks in the pit. The supervisor found nothing about it in pre-start notes for the ten days between 02/08 and the occurrence.

The supervisor would want a call at the spur but said the plan did not require one there. The supervisor had never pulled anyone up for not calling at an unlisted intersection, and said requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable. The nine intersections on the board were the whole of the practice on the pit.

The supervisor learned in about the middle of 2025 that alerts were switched off at the dig, after asking the technical services group why they had stopped. The supervisor did not know the geofence had been extended in June 2026 or that it now reached the ramp above the spur. The supervisor knew of no process for a light vehicle entering an operating pit, with no permit, call-in, board or check at the pit entry, so that anyone with a site access card could drive in. The supervisor described the dispatcher's handling of the emergency as textbook. The supervisor also said the haul truck operator was not well in the days after, and had told the contractor's health and safety adviser so.

Light vehicle driver

The light vehicle driver's account was that the driver slowed at the spur mouth, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, turning right to go back up the ramp. The driver put the speed coming out of the spur at about 25 km/h. The driver first said the vehicle had stopped and, on read-back, corrected this to slowed, and did not believe the vehicle came to a complete stop. The driver said the air was clear, that the driver could see the ramp surface and the windrow, and that the dust at Bindarra was nothing like the dust at other sites where the driver works.

Hazard report HAZ-2026-0917

The dewatering technician's hazard report of 04/08/2026 was submitted at 23:48, the same night as the near miss and seven days before the occurrence. The technician rated the hazard Medium. The report read in part:

He has not seen me and I have not seen him until I was already out on the road. I have reversed back into the road and let him go past."
  • "The problem is you cannot see up the ramp from that road. There is a rise in the ramp and a windrow along the side and you are out on the road before you can see anything. There is no sign on the ramp telling the trucks the road is there and there is no give way on our side. The closed sign that was there while they were building it has been taken away."
