The Dewatering Superintendent's closure entry of 06/08/2026 read:

  • "Spoke with the dewatering crew at pre-start 05/08 and reminded them to take care entering the main ramp and to give way to haul trucks at all times. Crew acknowledged. Trucks have right of way on the ramp per the traffic management plan. No further action required. Closed."

Analysis

The analysis follows the sequence from the works order to the convergence and the impact, then takes the matters that were examined and not settled. A factor found to have contributed to this occurrence is described as causal. A factor that increased risk without contributing to this occurrence is described as contributory.

Scope, and what the evidence excluded

The analysis had to settle how a light vehicle and a descending haul truck came to meet at an intersection that neither driver knew of, with neither able to see the other until six seconds remained. It also had to settle why none of the mine's controls for that interaction acted.

The qualifications and condition of the people and equipment were not in question. The haul truck operator had seven years on 220 t class rigid haul trucks, a verification of competency on type current from 06/2025 and an annual refresher in 02/2026. Drug and alcohol tests on the haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor were both negative.

The service brakes were tested at 0.80 m/s2 net on 03/08/2026, eight days before, and at 0.82 on 14/08/2026. The download of the occurrence gives 0.78 over the 4.6 seconds of braking, which is inside the scatter of the two tests. Brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds and the retarder went to maximum. No brake, retarder or park brake defect had been raised in the previous twelve months, and the pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 was complete with no defects. It was very unlikely that the service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration.

It was also very unlikely that the ramp surface was wet or slippery. The met station recorded no precipitation and the last rain at the site was 26 days earlier. The water cart's last pass on that section was at 01:10, and the investigator found the ramp dry throughout at 06:20. The braked scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked or sliding wheel, and the deceleration achieved matched the dry figures.

The occurrence was in darkness and the pit had no fixed lighting. No defect was raised against the truck's lighting in the previous twelve months, and the light vehicle's beacon lamp worked when tested after recovery. Darkness was therefore a condition of the shift and not a failure of equipment.

What worked

The haul truck operator's response was inside what the mine's own calculation assumes. The beacon came into view at 53 m, at the truck's last steady data point of 37 km/h at 02:47:06.0. Brake pressure began to rise at 02:47:07.4, a response of 1.4 seconds against the 1.5 seconds assumed in the plan's stopping distance calculation. The retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied in the same movement.

Braking took the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h. Because (24/37) squared is 0.42, about 58 per cent of the impact energy was removed. Steering right took the truck towards the wall and away from the pit edge, where the drop was more than 100 m. The operator explained the choice in interview: "If I go left I'm taking him with me, and there's nothing on that side, it's a hundred and something metres down. Right is the wall."

After the collision the haul truck operator called it in, stayed in the cab on dispatch's instruction until the ramp was stopped, then went down and stayed with the driver. Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic 49 seconds after the collision. The light vehicle's roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting but was not breached, and the driver's seatbelt was fastened and carried loading marks. These defences held, and they are the reason the injuries were limited to a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.

The sight line and what it left each driver

BIN-TMP-004 clause 6.2 reads: "At every intersection, the available sight distance shall be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle using the road at the posted speed, and in no case less than 120 m. Where this cannot be achieved, the intersection shall be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller."

The survey of 13/08/2026 gave 41 m of available sight distance. The stopping distance of a 220 t class truck empty at the posted 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descent, with a 1.5 second response, was 96 m. The intersection therefore met neither limb of the clause, and the second limb required it to be controlled.

The spur mouth lay 34 m below a convex grade break that the crews call the crest. An operator at an eye height of 5.80 m first had line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m. The top of a 4.5 m beacon whip on a vehicle approaching the mouth was in view from 53 m, but the vehicle's body was not. A driver at the mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first saw a descending truck at 38 m, because the 1.6 m inner windrow took the truck's lower body out of view before that.

The beacon was first visible six seconds before impact. On brakes alone from 37 km/h at the recorded 0.78 m/s2 the truck needed about 68 m to stop, so 53 m could not be enough whatever the response. With twice the sight line, the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the truck short of the spur. It was very likely that the sight line contributed to the collision. It was dangerous only because something was in it, and the conditions that follow explain how a vehicle came to be there.

The haul truck operator estimated in interview that the light vehicle was about forty metres away when first seen. The survey places the beacon at 53 m, and the download puts the truck at that point at its last steady data point. The estimate was of a distance seen for a second, and the survey is a measurement, so the survey was preferred. Either figure was far short of the 96 m the truck needed.

The sight line of 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m was a causal factor, because it left a truck at the posted speed unable to stop for anything at this intersection.

How an intersection with no controls came to exist

ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2 requires that "a management of change record shall be raised before any of the following", and the list begins with "a change to the mine's road network". Clause 5.3 excludes "routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced. Such work is managed under the works order."

Works order WO-26-4471 was raised on 28/07/2026 and approved on 29/07/2026. It cut 240 m of access road to bore DW-14 at RL 312, and the works were completed on 31/07/2026. It classified the work as "Routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design. No new plant or vehicle type. Management of change not required, ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3." Its handover field read "N/A". The three referrals at clause 5.4 exist only inside the management of change record. They are to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and to the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration. The works order form carries no equivalent fields, so none of the three was made.

The plan's owner was therefore not told of a new intersection that failed clause 6.2, and no stop control was provided. Clause 6.4 requires a warning sign, a give-way control and delineation, but only at intersections shown on the Schedule 1 road layout drawing. That drawing was dated 12/11/2025 and did not show the spur, so clause 6.4 did not reach it. The in-cab road network was last published on 24/07/2026, before the spur was completed. Publishing a revised network is a survey task raised by a management of change record, and none existed. The haul truck operator said the screen showed "Just the ramp" and that the operator would have expected a new road to appear, because "When they moved the ROM pad tip head last year that was on the screen the next night." Nobody compared the new intersection with the S4-LOAD suppression geofence, which already covered the place where the spur joined the ramp.

One point weighed against this. A referral is not itself a control, the plan's owner might have left the spur to the annual review, and no out-of-cycle review had been held in the plan's eleven years. However, the referrals are standing parts of the procedure. Of the fourteen new Stage 4 roads cut since the 12/11/2025 review, the three raised under a management of change record were all referred to the plan's owner, and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. A referral would have put in front of the plan's owner a survey showing the intersection failing clause 6.2, and would have put the intersection in front of the group that configures the geofence. That outweighed the possibility that the plan's owner would have waited for the annual review. It was very likely that opening the spur under a works order, with no referral, contributed to the collision.

The external guideline bears on a narrower path. MSG-14 clause 3.2 requires review of the plan at intervals not exceeding twelve months "and following any significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern". Clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate the intersections at which positive communication is required. The guideline defines neither "significant change" nor a basis for nomination, and it sets no minimum. Under clause 3.5 the plan is a site document that is not approved by the Inspectorate. The mine met the guideline on its face, because the plan had been reviewed within twelve months and nominated nine interaction zones.

The evidence supported two readings. One was that a defined trigger would have required the plan to be reopened when a road was added, and a stated basis for nomination would have given an intersection failing the sight distance rule a claim on the call list, so the guideline made doing nothing the default. The other was that the mine could have held an out-of-cycle review under its own clause 9.1 at any time and could have listed every intersection it had, so the guideline did not stop anyone. The evidence favoured the first reading only to the standard of proof. It was likely that the guideline's lack of a trigger and a basis contributed, and no more than that is claimed.

Opening the spur under a works order that referred nothing to anyone was a causal factor, because it removed the route by which the intersection would have reached the people responsible for the stop control, the map and the geofence. The guideline's lack of a review trigger and of a basis for nomination was a causal factor at the lower level of likelihood stated above.

The absence of a stop control and warning sign

At the time of the occurrence the intersection had no warning sign on either ramp approach, no stop or give-way control at the spur mouth, no delineation and no posted speed. The "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign was removed on 02/08/2026, the day the spur was first used, and nothing replaced it.

A stop at the mouth would have held the light vehicle there while the truck came into its driver's view. A dewatering technician came out of the same spur in front of a truck on 04/08/2026, reversed back in and let it pass. The haul truck operator said that a sign on the operator's side of the crest would have put the operator at about twenty and looking for the light vehicle: "If there'd been a sign on my side of that crest I'd have been at twenty and I'd have been looking for him."

Three points weighed against this. A stop line is only as good as the look from it, and from the mouth the view of 38 m was about four seconds of a truck at 37 km/h. The operator's view of what a sign would have done was formed after the event. A sign at an intersection that was not on the in-cab map would also have been a single cue. These points limit how much a sign would have achieved, but they do not remove it. It was likely that the missing stop control and warning sign contributed.

The absence of a stop control and warning sign at an intersection that failed the sight distance rule was a causal factor, at the level of likelihood stated above.

Positive calls

BIN-TMP-004 clause 4.3.1 requires that "a positive call shall be made on the relevant pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B", and that entry not be made until the call is acknowledged or the channel is confirmed clear. Clause 4.3.2 states: "At intersections not listed at Appendix B, vehicles shall give way in accordance with clause 4.1. No call is required." The note to Appendix B adds that an intersection is added "where it appears on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 and the review assesses it as requiring positive communication".

The spur was on neither Schedule 1 nor Appendix B. Nothing in the plan allowed an intersection to be added between reviews, and nothing required a new road to be referred to the plan's owner. The next date on which the spur could have been listed was 12/11/2026.

The pit channel recording shows the practice that followed. HT-407 called and was acknowledged at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28, at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37 and at the RL 360 crossover coming down at 02:46:21. That last call was 51 seconds before the collision. Neither vehicle made any transmission about the spur, the bore, or a light vehicle being in the Stage 4 pit. The haul truck operator, the light vehicle driver and the night shift supervisor each described the same practice, that calls are made at the nine intersections on the crib room board and nowhere else. The operator said "Nobody calls." The supervisor said a call would be wanted at the spur, that the plan did not require one at an unlisted intersection, that the supervisor had never pulled anybody up for not calling there, and that requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable.

Had the spur been listed, it was very likely that the call would have been made. The haul truck operator called at every listed intersection passed that night, and the channel was open with the light vehicle logged on to it at 18:04.

The call itself is a separate step. A call from either vehicle would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the supervisor, and under clause 4.3.1 entry was not to be made until the call was acknowledged or the channel confirmed clear. A call gives knowledge and not separation, and the two vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first across 41 m of sight line. That limits what a call could guarantee, but it would have changed what each driver knew before the truck reached the crest. It was likely that the absence of a call from either vehicle contributed.

The mine had other warnings. The technician's hazard report of 04/08/2026 described this interaction, with the rise, the windrow, no sign, no give-way and a truck about 60 m away that the technician judged did not know the road was there. It was closed on 06/08/2026 by the Dewatering Superintendent with a reminder to the crew, and the risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low. It was not referred to the mining department, the contractor, the survey department or the plan's owner. Three earlier reports, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, described a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at three other unlisted intersections. Each was closed within three days with a reminder, none was referred to the plan's owner, and none changed Appendix B, Schedule 1 or any physical control.

The plan's call requirement was a causal factor because it could be applied only at listed intersections and could be extended only at the annual review, so at this intersection it was not in force. The absence of a call from either vehicle was a causal factor, at the lower level of likelihood stated above.

Collision awareness

The collision awareness system on the Stage 4 haul fleet operated at Level 8, operator advisory. Level 9 intervention was available on the fleet and was not enabled at Bindarra. The system raised an advisory alert when a tag entered the 60 m ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, "except inside a suppression geofence. Inside a suppression geofence no alert is raised at any range, and the system logs a proximity event only once the range falls below 25 m."

The S4-LOAD geofence was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the loading face to stop nuisance alerts. It was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the face advanced, and the extension carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time, to a point 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection. The spur, cut seven weeks later, therefore joined the ramp inside the suppressed area. The extension was made by the contractor's technical services group as a configuration task, is not recorded in the traffic management plan and was not reviewed against it. The system logged the light vehicle at 02:47:09.2 at 21.4 m and 32 km/h closing, and the alert was suppressed.

The configuration, the log and the statistics come from the system itself. It was extremely likely that the operators did not know the geofence reached the ramp, because no training record anywhere on site covers the geofences. The haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor each said they did not know the system was off on the ramp, and the supervisor said the system was known to be off only at the dig. The system's statistics show how consistent the effect was. HT-407 raised 1,684 advisory alerts in the twelve months before the occurrence, all outside the geofence. Across the fleet 68 proximity events inside it were suppressed, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, and all nine dated after 09/06/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether other haul truck operators on the Stage 4 fleet held the same belief about the system]

The direct effect of the suppression was small. Unsuppressed, an alert would have sounded when the light vehicle's tag entered the 60 m ring, at about 02:47:06.5. That was half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on, so it would have told the operator what the operator was already reacting to. The system is advisory only and carries no intervention.

The effect on expectation was larger but could not be measured. The haul truck operator described it in interview: "I assumed there was nothing to go off at. You don't see light vehicles on that ramp at night, so if the thing's quiet, the road's empty." For the first ten of the operator's fourteen months that belief was sound, because the ramp was outside the geofence and nothing there had been alerted on. From June the system was silent whatever was on the road, and nobody told the operator. The operator came over the crest carrying that expectation, with no intersection on the screen and none on the road to indicate otherwise. Against this, the operator was descending at the speed every operator used on that ramp, and the operator's own remedy was a sign and not the system. The suppression likely contributed through that expectation, and the evidence supports that effect at the standard of proof and no higher.

The suppression of alerts at the spur by a geofence of which operators had not been told was a causal factor, through the expectation it created and not through the alert it withheld.

The light vehicle driver's access to the pit

ORR-STD-009 clause 7.4 states that equivalence of a contractor's induction "does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement, or to the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted". Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a card is issued.

The light vehicle driver's access card was issued on 09/08/2026 against the recognition agreement that Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical has held since 2023, after a 20 minute gatehouse briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. The gatehouse held no record of the supplement or the assessment and was not asked for one, and nothing in the access card system distinguished a person who might drive in an operating pit from one who might not. The training file records the Hallorn online module of 24/07/2026 and no pit driving assessment. The driver said they had never heard of the assessment and had never seen BIN-TMP-004. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site-specific supplement was issued to the driver]

The assessment is where a light vehicle driver is taught how the pit's traffic rules work in practice, including giving way to haul trucks, approaching an intersection that cannot be seen up, and when calls are made. The driver said that if they had been told to call, they would have called. Against this, the driver was already applying the first rule the assessment teaches, that light vehicles give way to heavy vehicles at all times, and slowed and looked before going out. The plan required no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught a call at RL 312. What the assessment would have added is how to approach a mouth that cannot be seen out of, which is to stop and look again and not merely to slow. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the content of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment] It was likely that issuing the card without a check for the assessment contributed, held below the other findings because of that gap and because the driver was already applying the first rule.

Issuing access cards with no check of the pit driving assessment was a causal factor, at the level of likelihood stated above.

The light vehicle driving out of the spur

The driver's account, corrected on read-back from stopped to slowed, was that they slowed at the mouth, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, turning right to go up the ramp. The driver put the speed coming out of the spur at about 25 km/h and did not believe they had come to a complete stop. The system log places the light vehicle at the spur mouth at 02:47:09.2, with the truck 21.4 m above it. The light vehicle's movements before the mouth, including its departure from the bore collar at about 02:45, rest on the driver's account alone.

The truck was within the 38 m the driver could see from the mouth from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the driver reached the mouth. The look up the ramp therefore came a second or two before the truck came over the crest, when it was beyond anything the position allowed the driver to see. A full stop at the mouth would very likely have shown the truck, and the driver would have let it pass, as the technician did on 04/08/2026. The 5 per cent allowance in the evidence is that a stop is only as good as the look from it, and the view from the mouth was 38 m.

Several points weighed against treating this as a decision that failed. The margin from a stop at 38 m was thin. The driver was applying the give-way rule in clause 4.1, which is the rule BIN-TMP-004 states for unlisted intersections, and the mouth carried no stop control, line, sign or posted speed. These points explain why slowing and looking was an understandable approach to this mouth. They do not alter that without the light vehicle on the ramp there is no collision. It was extremely likely that the light vehicle's driving out of the spur without stopping contributed to the collision.

The light vehicle's driving out of the spur onto the ramp without stopping was a causal factor, and it was the last step at which a different action would have avoided the collision.

Convergence and outcome

HT-407 was descending at 37 km/h with no intersection on its in-cab map, no warning sign on the approach, no call on the channel and no alert. The light vehicle was coming out of a spur whose mouth gave 38 m of sight line, with no give-way control and no call, and its driver did not know of the truck. The first sighting available to the haul truck operator was the beacon at 53 m, six seconds before the impact, and the driver's look came before the truck was in view. Neither the radio log, the download, the system log nor the interviews contain any indication that either driver knew of the other before then. The night shift supervisor did not know that a light vehicle was in the pit, and there was no permit, call-in or board by which the supervisor could have. It was extremely likely that the two vehicles converged with neither driver aware of the other until six seconds remained, and that nothing in those six seconds could have prevented the collision.

The spur joined the ramp on a descending truck's left, on the inside of a left-hand bend at 71 degrees, so the light vehicle turning right to go up the ramp crossed the descending lane with its right side towards the truck. The truck's front left struck it at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow. The accelerometer logged 1.9 g. Damage to the light vehicle was concentrated on its right side from the B pillar forward, and damage to the truck was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder. The data, the damage pattern and the debris field agree on the impact.

The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp. The gouge changed at 11.2 m from tyre scuff to body panel gouge, which is where the vehicle went over, and it came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, facing down-ramp. The door on the resting side was against the ground, so extrication was through the rear, 27 minutes after the collision. The structure and the restraint held, and the truck's right steering input kept the push running down the ramp towards the wall.

The convergence of the two vehicles with neither driver aware of the other was a causal factor, and the impact and roll-over that followed are the mechanism by which it produced the injuries.

Contributory risk: the roster

The contractor's Stage 4 haul roster was 14 nights on and 7 off, 18:00 to 06:30, within a fatigue management standard that permits up to 14 consecutive night shifts with a minimum 10 hour break. The haul truck operator was on night 10 of 14, and the collision at 02:47 was 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift, in the window of lowest circadian alertness. Every limit in the standard was met, and the previous nine shifts were worked in sequence with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes.

The roster could have affected the occurrence only through a slow or absent response, and the recorded data contradict that. The response was 1.4 seconds, inside the 1.5 seconds the plan assumes, and the braking and steering that followed were correct and immediate. Braking at the recorded 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m, a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h and not 24 km/h. The 1.4 seconds cost about 7 km/h of impact speed and not the collision. It was unlikely that the roster contributed to this occurrence.

It remains a risk worth acting on. The roster puts every haul truck operator at the wheel of a 220 tonne vehicle in the small hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night, where the defence against an unlit hazard at an unlisted intersection is the operator's own detection and response. At an intersection with a longer sight line than RL 312, a slower response could be the difference between stopping and not. It was likely that this exposure matters. The roster is treated here as a contributory risk and not as a factor in this occurrence.

Matters examined and not settled

Airborne dust above the intersection

The water cart's last pass on the section was at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the occurrence, against a standing 90 minute interval, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval against a shift mean of 88. The site trigger was 250. The haul truck operator described dust hanging on the ramp and said the cart had been through earlier and it dries out. The light vehicle driver was firm that the air was clear, but that account concerned the spur below the windrow, slow or stopped, and not the ramp above the crest where the truck was. It was likely that dust was in the air above the crest.

Whether it affected what the haul truck operator could see is a different question. Dust hanging in the truck's lights over the crest is the condition in which a driver picks out a beacon late. The 142 reading is a measure of particulate at a monitor head and not of what could be seen from either cab, and nothing at Bindarra measures visibility. The beacon was in view from 53 m, the first point at which the survey says it could be seen at all. The download puts the truck at that point at its last steady data point, and the 1.4 second response from there was inside the plan's allowance, which leaves little room for a delay. The operator could not say whether dust made a difference.

However, the sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and was not recorded, so the evidence cannot exclude dust costing a fraction of a second at the edge of the lights. Whether dust affected what the operator could see was as likely as not, and the evidence was evenly balanced. It could be settled only by a measurement of visibility from the cab on the night, and none exists. The matter is unresolved, and nothing from it is carried into the conclusions.

Haul truck operator fatigue

The haul truck operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift at 02:47, and inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. The operator's own voluntary sleep record gives 6 hours 30 minutes in the day before and between 5 and 7 hours on each of the preceding nine days. The operator described being tired "the way you are on night ten". The task on the approach was picking out a hazard in an unlit pit, which fatigue degrades first.

Against this, the operator said the tiredness was ordinary: "Not falling asleep tired ... I was awake and I was driving properly." Every limit in the fatigue standard was met, and the recorded performance shows none of the usual signs, with a 1.4 second response and braking and steering that were correct and immediate. Being tired on a tenth night is not the same as being fatigued to a degree that degrades performance. Whether the operator was fatigued on the approach was as likely as not, and the evidence was evenly balanced. A detailed fatigue assessment would be needed to settle it, and one was not pursued. Even had fatigue been shown, the braking arithmetic given for the roster would not change the outcome. The matter is unresolved, and nothing from it is carried into the conclusions.

Emergency response

The night shift was rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication begins, was called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse, in the second response vehicle that carried the hydraulic rescue tool. The second responder arrived with the tool at 03:07, and the driver was extricated at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision.

The post-incident review measured an extrication delay of approximately 9 minutes, from 02:58, when the primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made, to the second responder's arrival. It recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome because the injuries were stable and the driver was conscious throughout. The collision and the injuries were complete before the team was paged, so it was unlikely that the response time affected this occurrence or its outcome.

As a risk it is different. The night shift's extrication capability was one person plus a drive from the village, and nothing about the arrangement changes with the severity of a casualty. With a fuel fire, an unconscious casualty or an airway that needed the vehicle opened in the first ten minutes, the same nine minutes would be a different outcome. It was very likely that this structural gap matters as a risk.

Considered and not found contributing

Three matters were considered and not found to have contributed. The ramp surface was very unlikely to have been wet or slippery, on the evidence given at the start of this analysis. The service brakes were very unlikely to have delivered less than their tested deceleration, for the same reason. Airborne dust was examined and its effect could not be determined either way, as set out above, so it is not found to have contributed.

Conclusions

The investigation identified the following causal and contributory factors. They should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any organisation or individual.

Findings

  1. The guideline under which the mine's traffic management plan was made, MSG-14, did not define a significant change to the road network that would require the plan to be reviewed, and it set no basis for nominating the intersections at which a positive call is required. It was virtually certain that the guideline read this way, and the mine met it on its face. It was likely that this contributed, because a defined trigger and a stated basis would have given a new intersection a route onto the plan's call list between annual reviews. This conclusion is held at the standard of proof and no higher, because the mine could itself have reviewed the plan out of cycle or listed every intersection. (Safety issue)
  1. The RL 312 spur was virtually certain to have been cut under works order WO-26-4471, classified as routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design, so that no management of change record was raised and none of the three referrals that record would have triggered was made. These referrals were to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the in-cab road network and to the technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. This very likely contributed to the intersection having no stop control or warning sign and to the collision alerts being suppressed at the spur. Of the fourteen new Stage 4 roads cut since the last plan review, none of the eleven raised under a works order was referred to the plan's owner. (Safety issue)
  1. It was virtually certain that the plan required a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B, that an intersection could reach the list only through the annual reissue of the road layout drawing, and that nothing required a new road to be referred to the plan's owner. It was very likely that this contributed to neither driver making a call before the spur, because the truck operator called at every listed intersection passed that night, the last 51 seconds before the collision. (Safety issue)
  1. The collision awareness system fitted to HT-407 was very likely suppressed at the spur by the S4-LOAD geofence, which was extended up the main ramp on 09/06/2026 without review against the plan, and the truck operator and the night shift supervisor each said they did not know it was off on the ramp. It was likely that this contributed to neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. The mechanism was the truck operator's expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp. That effect could not be measured. The alert would have sounded at about 02:47:06.5, only about half a second after the beacon came into view, so it would have added little warning in itself. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the survey of whether other operators held the belief that the collision awareness system was active on the ramp] (Safety issue)
  1. The intersection had no stop control, warning sign, delineation or posted speed, although the available sight distance of 41 m failed the plan's clause 6.2 requirement. This was virtually certain, and the construction sign at the mouth was removed on 02/08/2026 and not replaced. It was likely that this contributed to the light vehicle driving out of the spur, although the margin from a stop at the mouth was thin, at 38 m of sight line. (Safety issue)
  1. Site access cards were virtually certain to have been issued against the contractor's recognition agreement with no check that the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment had been completed, and the light vehicle driver had not done it. It was likely that this contributed to the driver leaving the spur without stopping. The driver was already applying the give-way rule and the plan required no call at an unlisted intersection, which limits how far the assessment could have changed what the driver did. (Safety issue)
  1. The sight line at the spur was virtually certain to have been 41 m to the spur mouth and 53 m to the beacon, against a stopping distance of 96 m for the truck. It was very likely that this contributed to neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest.
  1. It was virtually certain that neither driver made a positive call, and none was required at the unlisted spur. It was likely that this contributed to the lack of awareness between them. A call would have given each vehicle knowledge of the other, although a call alone would not have separated them over 41 m of sight line.
  1. The light vehicle was virtually certain to have been driven out of the spur onto the ramp at about 25 km/h, without a complete stop, and it was very likely that this contributed to the collision. The truck came within the driver's 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the driver reached the mouth. A stop at the mouth would therefore very probably have shown the driver the truck.
  1. It was very likely that neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, and very likely that this contributed to the collision, because only about six seconds remained from the first sighting of the beacon at 53 m. The light vehicle's movements before it reached the spur mouth rest on the driver's account alone.
  1. The truck's front left was virtually certain to have struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h at 02:47:12, and with virtual certainty this was the mechanism by which the convergence became an injury.
  1. The light vehicle was virtually certain to have been pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side, and with virtual certainty this produced the driver's injuries, a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.
  1. The haul operators' roster of fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts virtually certainly existed and met every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard. It was unlikely that it contributed to this occurrence, because the recorded 1.4 second response was inside the 1.5 seconds the plan allows. It was likely that the roster increased risk generally. (Safety issue)
  1. The truck operator virtually certainly braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view, and this very likely reduced risk by lowering the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h and keeping the light vehicle against the pit side windrow.
  1. A wet or slippery ramp surface was very unlikely.
  1. A shortfall in the truck's service brake performance was very unlikely.

Causal factors

The causal factors began with the way the spur was created, and each led to the next. The works order opened the spur with no referral to anyone. That left the intersection without a stop control or warning sign and left the in-cab map without the road. It also left a geofence, extended up the ramp a few weeks earlier, silencing the collision alerts at the spur. The plan's call list, the card process and the guideline had already settled who would be expected to call, who would be carded to drive in the pit, and who would review the plan. Together these conditions led to the drive-out, then to the convergence, the impact and the roll-over.

  • The RL 312 spur was opened under a works order, so nothing was referred to the plan's owner, the survey department or the technical services group. This was virtually certain, and it very likely contributed to the absence of controls and to the alert suppression. (Safety issue)
  • There was no stop control or warning sign at an intersection that failed the sight distance rule. This was virtually certain, and it likely contributed to the light vehicle driving out of the spur. (Safety issue)
  • Collision alerts were suppressed at the spur by a geofence of which operators knew nothing. This was very likely, and it likely contributed to neither driver being aware of the other. The effect on the truck operator's expectation could not be measured, and the alert itself would have added little time. (Safety issue)
  • Positive calls were required only at listed intersections, and intersections were added only at the annual review. This was virtually certain, and it very likely contributed to neither driver making a call. (Safety issue)
  • Access cards were issued with no check of the pit driving assessment. This was virtually certain, and it likely contributed to the drive-out. (Safety issue)
  • MSG-14 set no review trigger and no basis for the positive-call list. This was virtually certain, and it likely contributed. It is held at the standard of proof and no higher. (Safety issue)
  • The sight line of 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m was virtually certain, and it very likely contributed to neither driver being aware of the other.
  • Neither driver made a positive call. This was virtually certain, and it likely contributed to the lack of awareness between them.
  • The light vehicle drove out of the spur without stopping. This was virtually certain, and it very likely contributed to the collision.
  • Neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. This was very likely, and it very likely contributed to the collision.
  • The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h. This was virtually certain, and it was virtually certain to have been the mechanism of the injury.
  • The light vehicle was pushed 18 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side. This was virtually certain, and it was virtually certain to have produced the injuries.

Contributory factors

  • Haul operators were rostered for fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts. This was virtually certain. It was unlikely to have contributed to this occurrence, because the truck operator's response of 1.4 seconds was inside the plan's allowance and a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24 km/h. It was likely to have increased risk, because the roster puts operators at the wheel in the small hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night. (Safety issue)

Other findings

  • The truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view. This was virtually certain, and it very likely reduced risk. Braking took the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h, and the steering turned the truck away from the open edge towards the wall.
  • The arrangement for night shift extrication is a matter still under examination. On the evidence so far, it was virtually certain that the second responder had to be called in from the village, and that extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes. It was unlikely that this affected the occurrence or its outcome, and very likely that the arrangement is a structural gap in a last-line defence.
  • Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection is a matter still under examination. On the evidence so far, dust was likely present, because the water cart pass was 7 minutes overdue and the monitor reading of 142 micrograms per cubic metre exceeded the shift mean of 88, although it was below the site trigger of 250. Whether it affected the sighting was about as likely as not. The beacon was in view from 53 m, which is the geometric limit, and the light vehicle driver described the air as clear. However, the sighting was inferred from the survey and not recorded, so a loss of a fraction of a second could not be excluded.
  • Whether the truck operator was fatigued during the approach could not be determined. It was about as likely as not. The truck operator was on night 10 of 14 and described being tired, but the recorded response was inside the plan's allowance and every limit in the fatigue standard was met. A detailed fatigue assessment would be needed to settle it. It was not pursued, because even had fatigue been shown, a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision.
  • A wet or slippery ramp surface was very unlikely. The surface was dry, no rain had fallen for 26 days, and the deceleration achieved matched the dry figure.
  • A shortfall in the service brakes was very unlikely. Tests eight days before and three days after gave 0.80 and 0.82 m/s2, and the occurrence gave 0.78.

Safety action and recommendations

This section describes the action organisations had taken or begun in response to the occurrence, says which safety issue each action answers and to what extent, and then sets out the recommendations for the issues that remain unaddressed.

Safety action taken

Site-wide direction on positive calls

At 05:10 on 12/08/2026, two hours twenty-three minutes after the collision, the Mining Manager of Orrabinda Resources issued a site-wide direction. It requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, whether or not the traffic management plan lists it, until further notice. The direction was read at the following four pre-starts and posted beside the Appendix B board in the Stage 4 crib room.

This answers the safety issue that positive calls were required only at listed intersections, and that an intersection was added only at the annual review, in part. For the Stage 4 pit it removes the dependence on Appendix B, so a call would now be required at an intersection such as the RL 312 spur. The direction stands only until BIN-TMP-004 is amended, and the plan itself still provides no route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews. The issue therefore remains open and is addressed by the second recommendation below.

Closure of the spur and survey of the other unlisted roads

The RL 312 spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic on the night of the occurrence and has remained closed. On 14/08/2026 the survey department measured the available sight distance at the other ten unlisted roads cut in Stage 4 since the last plan review. This was before the November reissue of Schedule 1. Two of the ten were below the clause 6.2 minimum and have been closed pending a stop control. Both remain open as actions.

This answers the safety issue that no stop control or warning sign was provided at an intersection failing the sight distance rule, in part. The closure removes the hazard at RL 312, and the survey and the two closures deal with the same hazard at the other roads examined. They do not change how a new road in Stage 4 reaches a survey or a control in the first place, which the first recommendation addresses.

Reporting of suppressed proximity events

On 28/08/2026 Tarrowen technical services added suppressed proximity events to the monthly collision awareness report, broken down by geofence and by vehicle class. They also re-cut the previous twelve months on the same basis for the Stage 4 fleet. In that period 68 proximity events inside the S4-LOAD geofence were suppressed, and nine of them involved a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary. They had been recorded and visible in the system throughout and had never been reported to anybody. The Technical Services Manager of Tarrowen Mining Services owns the action, which is in progress, with the first report due 30/09/2026.

This answers the safety issue of collision alerts suppressed at the spur by a geofence that operators knew nothing of, in part. It makes suppression visible to management. It does not tell operators where the system is suppressed, and it does not make a change to a suppression boundary subject to review, so the third recommendation remains.

Issues with no action recorded

For the safety issue that the spur was opened under a works order, so that nothing was referred to anyone, no action was recorded. It is addressed by the first recommendation.

Safety recommendations

The three recommendations below were raised on 01/09/2026 by the investigator in charge. All are open, with responses due on 30/09/2026.

Works orders that create a new intersection with a haul road

The management of change procedure ORR-PRO-022 excludes routine earthworks under a works order at clause 5.3, so the three referrals that clause 5.4 attaches to a management of change record were not made when the RL 312 spur was cut. Those referrals go to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and to the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. Of the fourteen new roads cut in Stage 4 since the review of 12/11/2025, the three raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner and none of the eleven raised under a works order was.

Recommendation: [NOT ESTABLISHED: the organisation to which this recommendation is addressed] should ensure that no new intersection with a haul road is created without referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration. This may be achieved either by ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 no longer excluding earthworks that create such an intersection, or by the works order form at Schedule 4 carrying the three clause 5.4 referrals.

Route for adding an intersection to Appendix B between reviews

BIN-TMP-004 adds an intersection to Appendix B only where it appears on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1, and Schedule 1 is reissued only at the annual review. No provision requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner when it is cut, so nothing anyone did could have armed the plan's positive call requirement at the RL 312 spur. The next date on which the spur could have been listed was 12/11/2026, three months after the collision.

Recommendation: [NOT ESTABLISHED: the organisation to which this recommendation is addressed] should ensure that BIN-TMP-004 provides a route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews, and that it requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner when it is opened to traffic.

Suppression geofence boundaries and operator knowledge

The S4-LOAD boundary moved 180 m up-ramp on 09/06/2026 as a system configuration task. Nobody outside the group that moved it was told, and no training for any person on site covers the geofences.

Recommendation: [NOT ESTABLISHED: the organisation to which this recommendation is addressed] should ensure that a change to a suppression geofence boundary is treated as a change to a documented control under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2, and that operators are told in writing where the collision awareness system is suppressed and why.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: responses to the three recommendations]

Suggestions from those interviewed

The haul truck operator suggested a sign on the intersection, the road shown on the in-cab map, and operators being told where the collision awareness system is switched off. The night shift supervisor suggested a permit, a call-in or some other means by which the supervisor of an operating pit knows which light vehicles are in it. The supervisor raised this as the change most wanted. These suggestions are the views of those interviewed and are not recommendations of the investigation.
